newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Kohl to hit back at critics in speech.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Kohl to hit back at critics in speech.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl, under fire over his government's handling of Germany's jobs crisis and big tax and pension reforms, plans to hit back at his critics when he delivers a key address to parliament on Friday.

Kohl will give "a fighting speech" to rally his Christian Democrat (CDU) party and launch a broadside at the opposition, which he believes is blocking vital reforms, an adviser told Reuters on Thursday.
The 66-year-old chancellor had resisted calls by the Social Democrat-led (SPD) opposition for a parliamentary debate on what his centre-right alliance would do to fight unemployment.
But, facing dole queues set to reach a new post-war record of 4.5 million this winter, Kohl this week changed his mind.

Internal criticism of Kohl's leadership has mounted ever since a group of up-and-coming provincial CDU leaders -- dubbed the "wild bunch" by German media -- attacked coalition proposals to reform the tax system earlier this month.
Kohl, whose grip over even local CDU branches is legendary, managed only with difficulty to quell that uprising.

But party attacks have resurfaced with renewed vigour this week over separate plans by Labour Minister Norbert Bluem -- who has been in the cabinet since Kohl came to power in 1982 -- to rejig Germany's compulsory state pensions scheme.

Although no one has publicly criticised Kohl, the attacks intensified on Thursday when the Sueddeutsche Zeitung daily led its front page with a story headlined "Massive Criticism against Kohl from the CDU Leadership".

The newspaper's report, without naming names, said party leaders were upset by Kohl's "clumsy" handling of the tax and pensions debate. They also said that Kohl had run out of ideas on how to turn Germany's economy around.
"Kohl feels that he is up against the wall and can't make any more moves," the paper quoted a senior party official as saying. "What should he say?"
Kohl's lack of interest in the details of economic policy is well known. But he can see when the political message behind the reforms is not getting across.
His decision to leave his allies to squabble for months over plans to reduce taxes has fuelled voter scepticism over whether they will actually end up better off or not.

Opinion polls show voters see recent talk about raising value-added tax to offset the 30 billion marks ($18.28 billion) in tax cuts Finance Minister Theo Waigel plans as a sign the whole effort will add up to little more than fiscal sleight-of-hand.
In addition to public doubts about Kohl's tax pledges, there is also a credibility gap within his own team over his bid to halve unemployment by the turn of the century, newspaper commentators wrote.
The Die Woche weekly said Kohl's jobs pledge was "not seriously believed by anyone in the government camp".
"Every month there are more to halve, because the number of jobless keeps rising rather than falling," it wrote.
Kohl, who wants to steer Germany to the completion of European monetary union (EMU), has not said publicly whether he will run for a record fifth term in autumn 1998.
His coalition lineup trails a possible alliance of SPD and Greens in the polls, and signs are mounting that his personal popularity is on the slide.

In a Forsa institute survey for Die Woche, Germans were asked who they would choose as chancellor if the post were decided by direct election. Kohl beat SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine by 35 percent to 23 percent.

But if Kohl faced Gerhard Schroeder, the Eurosceptic SPD premier of Lower Saxony state, he would come off loser by a 31 to 41 percent margin. Over a tenth of Kohl's own party backers in the 2,500 survey sample said they would vote for Schroeder.
